title: Artificial island
label: idb
statement:
Given a 1D array:

1 = land
0 = ocean

You have a limited amount of material that can convert ocean cells into land.

Find the maximum possible island size.

Follow-ups:
1. Circular array
2. Obstacles represented by -1
3. Variable ocean depth / conversion cost

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Given a 1D array:
> 
> 1 = land
> 0 = ocean
> 
> You have a limited amount of material that can convert ocean cells into land.
> 
> Find the maximum possible island size.
> 
> Follow-ups:
> 1. Circular array
> 2. Obstacles represented by -1
> 3. Variable ocean depth / conversion cost

A row of cells, some land and some ocean. You may convert up to `material` ocean cells into land. An island is a **contiguous** run of land. How long is the longest run you can produce.

One integer: the length of the best achievable run. Not which cells to convert, though the window bounds give you that for free.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| `material` counts cells, each costing 1. | If it is a quantity of earth and cells have depths, that is follow-up 3 already and the base answer changes. **This is the clarification to ask**, especially since the examples that would have settled it are missing. |
| Cells are only 0 or 1 in the base problem. | -1 appears in follow-up 2 and is a different beast: it can never become land at any price. |
| `material` may exceed the number of ocean cells. | Then the answer is the whole array. The window logic gives that without a special case, which is worth pointing out rather than adding an `if`. |
| An empty array returns 0. | Not 1, and not an exception. Cheap to state and the first thing a test checks. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
Rewrite the problem before solving it. "Convert at most k ocean cells to maximise a contiguous run of land" is the same sentence as **"find the longest subarray containing at most k zeros"**. The conversion is a red herring: you never need to decide *which* cells to convert, because inside any window you would obviously convert all of them.

That reframing is the whole insight, and it is worth doing out loud, because it turns a planning problem into a counting one.

Now, why two pointers rather than checking every window. The window is valid while it contains at most k zeros, and **adding a cell never makes a window valid and removing one never makes it invalid**. That monotonicity means once the window at `left` has failed for a given `right`, it has failed for every larger `right` too — so `left` never needs to move backwards. Each pointer crosses the array once and the whole thing is O(n).

Say that monotonicity argument explicitly. Plenty of candidates produce the two-pointer code from memory; the ones who can say why the left pointer is allowed to be forward-only are the ones who can adapt it when follow-up 2 breaks the assumption.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** For every start and every end, count the zeros in that window; if the count is within budget, record the length. *O(n³) naively, or O(n²) with a running count as the end extends. O(1) space.*

**Why not good enough.** At n = 100,000 — a plausible size for a coastline scan — O(n²) is ten billion operations. But the more useful observation is that the O(n²) version is already *doing* the sliding window, just restarting it from every left position. Noticing that the restart is unnecessary is the step to O(n), and framing it that way makes the optimisation feel derived rather than recalled.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | `int[] cells` of 0s and 1s, and an integer `material` |
| TRANSFORMATION | "Convert at most k cells" becomes "tolerate at most k zeros inside the window". Nothing is actually converted. |
| DATA STRUCTURE | Two indices and one counter. No collection at all. |
| ALGORITHM | Extend `right`, counting zeros. While the count exceeds the budget, advance `left`, decrementing when it leaves a zero. Record the best length at every step. |
| OUTPUT | The largest window length seen |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Set `best = 0`, `ocean = 0`, `left = 0`.
- For each `right`: if `cells[right] == 0`, increment `ocean`.
- While `ocean > material`: if `cells[left] == 0`, decrement `ocean`; then `left++`.
- Set `best = max(best, right - left + 1)`.
- Return `best`.

- The island must be contiguous. That is what makes this a window problem rather than a counting problem — if gaps were allowed the answer would just be `ones + material`.
- You may use **fewer** than `material` conversions. The best window is not necessarily the one that spends everything.
- Conversion cost is uniform in the base problem: one unit per ocean cell. Follow-up 3 breaks exactly that.
- One pass, O(1) extra space, is achievable and is what the question is looking for.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| Two indices, no collection | The only state the validity test needs is *how many* zeros are in the window, not which. A queue of zero positions would also work and would be strictly worse — more memory for no new capability. |
| A single counter | Updated on entry and on exit. This is the piece that generalises: in follow-up 3 it becomes a cost sum, and in `76 Minimum Window Substring` it becomes a multiset. The shape of the loop does not change. |
| `while`, not `if`, on the shrink | With uniform costs one step is always enough, so `if` happens to work. With weighted costs it is not, and a `while` that was correct all along is better than one you have to remember to change. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**Why the shrink loop is a `while`.** When the window goes over budget, advancing `left` once may remove a **land** cell, which does not reduce the zero count. The loop has to keep going until the window is affordable again. An `if` passes the obvious tests and fails on runs of land before a zero.

**Why `best` is recorded every iteration.** Not only when the window grows. After a shrink the window is smaller, and `Math.Max` keeps the earlier answer. Recording only on growth is a subtle bug that produces the right answer whenever the best window happens to be last.

**The circular version: why two copies, and why the cap.** Walking `2n` cells lets a window wrap the join. Without `right - left + 1 > n` in the shrink condition, a window could wrap all the way round and count cells twice — reporting an island longer than the array. The early return when the whole ring is affordable is there for the same reason and is not just an optimisation: with `material` covering every ocean cell, the window would otherwise try to exceed `n`.

**The obstacle version: why the window resets rather than shrinks.** A `-1` cannot be converted at any price, so no valid window may contain one. That is categorically different from an expensive cell. `left = right + 1; ocean = 0;` cuts the array in two at that point. Trying to express an obstacle as "infinite cost" and reusing the weighted version would also work, and is worse — it invites overflow and hides the structure.

**The weighted version: why the same two pointers still work.** Costs are non-negative, so the window cost is still monotonic in the window bounds: growing can only increase it, shrinking can only decrease it. That is the **only** property the forward-only `left` pointer relies on. If any cost could be negative the technique collapses entirely and it becomes a prefix-sum problem.

**`long spent`, not `int`.** n cells at a per-cell cost can overflow a 32-bit sum on large inputs. `budget` stays an `int` because it is compared, not accumulated. Cheap, and the kind of thing the Staff Coding module explicitly says it looks for.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MaxIsland` | O(n) | O(1) | Each pointer advances at most n times; the shrink is amortised |
| `MaxIslandCircular` | O(n) | O(1) | Two passes over n, still linear; no array copy is made |
| `MaxIslandWithObstacles` | O(n) | O(1) | A reset is O(1); the total work is still one pass |
| `MaxIslandWeighted` | O(n) | O(1) | Same loop with a sum instead of a count |

**The shrink loop looks nested but is not O(n²).** `left` only ever increases, so across the entire run the inner loop executes at most n times in total. That is an amortised argument and it is the one to state, because the code visually contains a loop inside a loop and an interviewer may be waiting to see whether you notice.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Empty array | Returns 0 in all four variants, checked first. |
| `material = 0` | Degenerates to "longest existing run of 1s", which the same loop produces with no special case. |
| `material >=` the number of ocean cells | Returns `n`. Falls out of the loop; the circular version needs the explicit early return. |
| All ocean, material short | Returns exactly `material`. |
| All land | Returns `n` with no conversions used. |
| Single cell `[0]` with `material = 0` | Returns 0. The window is never valid, so `best` stays at its initial 0. |
| Circular, whole ring affordable | Returns `n`, via the early return — without it the window would wrap past `n`. |
| Obstacle at index 0 or at the end | Handled: the reset sets `left` past the array end harmlessly, and the loop terminates normally. |
| All obstacles | Returns 0. No window can contain a `-1`, so none is ever valid. |
| Weighted, a cost that overflows `int` | Accumulated in a `long`. |

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md: **Verification exercise:** Off-by-one / window logic — The window length is `right - left`, not `right - left + 1` — every answer is one short. (The single `if` shrink is actually fine here because the window never needs to shrink by more than one per step; the off-by-one is the bug.) "all land" returns 2 instead of 3.

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**What if the array is circular?**

Iterate `right` from 0 to `2n - 1`, indexing with `% n`. Add one clause to the shrink condition: `|| right - left + 1 > n`, so the window can never exceed the array length. Then handle the degenerate case first — if every ocean cell is affordable the answer is `n`, and returning early avoids the window trying to wrap onto itself.

*Trade-off:* Two passes instead of one, still O(n), still O(1) space because no copy is materialised — `% n` is doing the concatenation. The alternative, actually building a 2n array, is simpler to read and doubles the memory; at this size I would take the modulo.

**What if some cells are obstacles, represented by -1?**

No valid window may contain a `-1`, so the array becomes a set of independent segments separated by obstacles. On meeting one, reset: `left = right + 1`, `ocean = 0`. Each segment is then the original problem, and the shared `best` across all of them is the answer.

*Trade-off:* This is the follow-up that most rewards saying what changed conceptually. Modelling `-1` as infinite cost and reusing the weighted version gives the right answer and obscures the reason; the reset says "the window cannot cross this" in code.

**What if each ocean cell has its own conversion cost?**

Replace the zero **count** with a cost **sum**, and compare against the budget instead of against k. The loop is otherwise unchanged. Accumulate in a `long`.

*Trade-off:* No cost at all: same time, same space, same shape. Which is the point worth making — the generalisation is free precisely because the original solution was built on the right invariant. If costs could be **negative** the technique would collapse and this would become a prefix-sum problem with a very different answer.

**Return which cells to convert, not just the length.**

Track `bestLeft` and `bestRight` whenever `best` is updated. The cells to convert are the zeros in that range. If several windows tie, any of them is correct — say so, and say which one you return (the first, here).

*Trade-off:* Two extra integers. The only real decision is tie-breaking, and stating that ties exist is better than silently returning one.

**It is 2-D now — a grid, and you can convert k water cells.**

Contiguity in 2-D is connectivity, not an interval, so there is no window to slide. For k = 1 there is a good O(rc) solution: flood-fill to label every island with its size, then for each water cell sum the sizes of its distinct neighbouring labels and add one. For general k it is far harder and I would not claim a clean algorithm.

*Trade-off:* The k = 1 case is a genuinely nice problem and worth knowing (it is LeetCode 827). For general k I would say plainly that I do not have a polynomial approach in mind rather than improvise one, and ask whether k = 1 is the intended case.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Empty array? All ocean? Material larger than the array?* — 0; min(material, n); n

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Brute force vs this?* — O(n²) or O(n³) vs O(n) window
- *Why does a window work?* — The constraint is monotone: a window valid now stays valid when shrunk
